notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 39. I ran out of search and fetch requests before I could check some sources, so there are gaps:
- I didn't reach preceptaustin.org's page on this psalm or Barnes.
- I found nothing from a Wesleyan/Methodist, Lutheran or Orthodox writer.
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this psalm.

Those areas are left out as you asked. I've marked where a tradition's view comes only from a search-result excerpt rather than the full page.

**Sources (short names used below)**
- **EW**: Enduring Word (David Guzik, Calvary Chapel / charismatic-leaning evangelical), https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-39/
- **Gill**: John Gill (Baptist), https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/39.htm
- **Pulpit**: Pulpit Commentary (Anglican), https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/39.htm
- **Ellicott**: Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican; excerpt only), https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-39.html
- **Calvin**: John Calvin (Reformed; excerpt only), https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/39.htm
- **Henry**: Matthew Henry (Presbyterian/Nonconformist; excerpt only), https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_039.cfm
- **Spurgeon**: C. H. Spurgeon's Treasury of David (Baptist; excerpt only), https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps039.cfm
- **Expositor's**: Expositor's Bible (excerpt only), https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-39.html
- **Illustrator**: Biblical Illustrator (excerpt only), https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-39.html
- **NET**: NET Bible notes, https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=39
- **Augustine**: Augustine's Exposition on Psalm 39 (Catholic), https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801039.htm

---

**Title (v. 1a)**
- Jeduthun was most likely the chief musician David appointed for temple praise (1 Chr 16:41), also called Ethan. Some Jewish interpreters thought the word meant an instrument or a tune. Suggested settings include Absalom's revolt, when Shimei cursed David (Theodoret), or some painful discipline. — Gill
- EW: the psalm can't be tied to any particular event in David's life. — EW
- *Catholic (Augustine):* he takes "Idithun" to mean "over-leaping them." It stands for the believer who rises above people whose hearts are fixed on passing earthly things, and any reader can be that person. — Augustine

**v. 1**
- David decided not to voice his doubts in front of the wicked, who would take his words as criticism of God. Kidner and Boice are cited for this. Spurgeon is cited too: publicising a believer's doubts would be doing the devil's work. — EW
- He would rather suffer in silence than say anything the ungodly could treat as grumbling against God's providence. — Ellicott
- Gill lists sins of the tongue, especially those tempting in hard times: envy of the wicked who prosper, impatience, and grumbling at God's hand. "While the wicked is before me" could mean Absalom and Shimei, or seeing the wicked prosper, or ungodly visitors to his sickbed. — Gill
- The "bridle" means holding back impatience. The Pulpit sees no link with the silence of Ps 38:13–14 and prefers the Prayer Book wording, "while the ungodly is in my sight." — Pulpit
- EW, by contrast, does compare it with Ps 38:13: there David stayed silent rather than defend himself, here he stays silent about his doubts. — EW
- Calvin: David was surrounded by enemies who mocked his every sigh. He guarded himself because he knew his own weakness and Satan's schemes. Readers should likewise keep their feelings in check when trouble comes. — Calvin
- NET: a lament spoken in front of evil men could be sinful if it gave them a reason to insult God. — NET

**v. 2**
- "Even from good": the Pulpit gives two readings. Either "I kept quiet, but it did me no good," or "I kept back even good words" (the Prayer Book's reading). Holding in strong feeling makes the pain worse. — Pulpit
- Gill weighs three options:
  - He said nothing good or bad, for fear something wrong would slip out.
  - His silence went too far and became wrong, since he didn't pray or give thanks.
  - (Gill's preference) He didn't defend his cause before men and left it to God.

  Gill also reports the Targum's view that he fell silent "from the words of the law." — Gill
- David found it easier to say nothing than to speak wisely. Spurgeon is quoted: total silence was a safe way to avoid sin, unless it meant failing in his duty to speak well of God. — EW
- The Septuagint and Vulgate say his sorrow was "renewed." — Ellicott
- NET: he held back the urge to get relief by voicing his lament. — NET
- *Augustine:* afraid of speaking evil, he stopped speaking good, and he came to condemn his own decision. — Augustine

**v. 3**
- Quoting VanGemeren, EW says "hot" and "fire" are images of anger: the more he brooded, the angrier he got. Here silence was not golden. — EW
- Gill rules out zeal or love for God as the fire. He reads it as passion and resentment. When David spoke, he broke his vow and spoke rashly. — Gill
- Calvin: "spake with my tongue" is a frank confession that he had complained out loud. Even a champion like David failed, and Satan attacks hardest those who try to obey God. — Calvin
- He burst out in speech and made his moan to God. — Pulpit
- *Augustine:* he spoke to God, not to the hearers who picked at his words, so that God would teach him. — Augustine

**v. 4**
- David broke his silence in the best way, by praying to God rather than talking to people. G. Campbell Morgan is cited: this isn't a request to know the date of his death but to grasp how short life is. — EW
- Gill gives the opposite reading: an impatient wish to die, like Job's (Job 7:15). Saints sometimes wish for death in a fretful mood, and it is rare to wish for it rightly, as Paul did (Phil 1:23). — Gill
- The Pulpit puts it between the two. Like Job but not quite: tired of life, David asks how long he must go on bearing it. Hengstenberg's rendering, "when I shall cease," is noted. — Pulpit
- Calvin finds irony here. The point is that the few years left could never make up for his suffering. — Calvin
- The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "leave off" and implies ceasing to live. "Frail" is the better translation. — Ellicott
- Henry: our earthly "house" is wearing out, so we should prepare for a "house not made with hands." — Henry
- *Augustine:* "my end" is the goal not yet reached, the one Paul pressed toward (Phil 3:12–13), beyond a life of trials and critics. — Augustine

**v. 5**
- A handbreadth was one of Israel's smallest measures, a couple of inches (VanGemeren). Even David, warrior, poet and king, was only vapour. Selah invites us to stop and think how short life is. — EW
- A handbreadth is four fingers wide, the width of a hand. A life is nothing next to God's eternity, but life in the world to come lasts forever. "Every man at his best state" covers rich and poor, and even Adam before the Fall. The believer's spiritual standing in Christ, though, is not subject to vanity. — Gill
- It seems odd that someone weary of life should complain that it is short, but people are like that (compare Job 14). Many scholars translate "ordained for utter vanity." — Pulpit
- Henry: all of time is nothing beside God's eternity. — Henry
- Spurgeon's Treasury quotes Nathanael Hardy on the handbreadth, comparing a life with eternity. It also has extended notes on Selah. — Spurgeon
- The Hebrew allows "all mankind, though seemingly secure, is a vapor." — NET

**v. 6**
- The verse sounds like Ecclesiastes: people are busy, but in vain and without substance. — EW
- "In an image" means a mere appearance of life without the reality (compare Job 27, Eccl 2). — Pulpit
- Gill surveys the meanings of "image" or "shadow." He links it to the unregenerate walking in darkness, but most of all to the passing show of the great. — Gill
- NET: people are like ghosts, here today and gone tomorrow. The text as it stands is awkward, and NET follows an emendation reading "vain things of wealth." — NET
- Henry: if the world is like this, God keep me from seeking my portion in it. — Henry
- *Augustine:* he challenges the covetous person who stores up treasure "for my children." Augustine calls that excuse the voice of parental love but also a cover for injustice. — Augustine

**v. 7**
- Seeing how frail life is turned David's hope to God. Morgan: real life is desire and expectation centred on God. — EW
- Not long life, human help or riches, but God himself. Here the psalmist "comes to his right mind." — Gill
- It sounds like a cry of despair, but faith answers, "My hope is in thee." — Pulpit
- Ellicott: the psalmist had no hope of immortality to turn to, because it "had not yet dawned." His comfort was God's mercy and his own moral deliverance. — Ellicott
- Calvin: no one truly hopes in God until he feels his own frailty and is brought to nothing. — Calvin

**v. 8**
- He looked to God, not himself, to free him from sin, like Paul in Romans 7:24–8:4. — EW
- Gill reads this as a full deliverance:
  - from sin's power, by grace
  - from its guilt, by Christ's blood
  - from punishment, because Christ bore the curse
  - and finally from sin itself

  "The foolish" means scoffers in general. — Gill
- Coming near to God sharpens the sense of sin, so pardon comes first. Then he asks that his punishment end, so that fools may not mock him. — Pulpit
- Calvin: he no longer grumbles. He admits many sins and declares God righteous. — Calvin

**v. 9**
- Gill offers three possible times: his first silence, a silence he returned to, or one he now resolves to keep. The reason is that God is the author of affliction (though not of sin), as in Amos 3:6. Gill rejects Augustine's reading, "because thou hast made me." — Gill
- Knowing the suffering was God's just punishment helped him stay silent. — Pulpit
- VanGemeren, cited by EW: a personal God, not an impersonal force, is in charge of his life. — EW
- Writers quoted in Spurgeon's Treasury: this is God training his children, "the discipline of love" with no wrath in it. Because it is the Lord's doing, it can be taken kindly, patiently and thankfully. — Spurgeon

**v. 10**
- Asking God to take the blow away doesn't contradict the silence of v. 9, because only God can remove it. — Gill
- The Hebrew reads "the quarrel of thine hand." — Pulpit
- NET translates "You have almost beaten me to death!" — NET
- EW quotes Maclaren: saying "Hold! enough!" to God can be presumption or a child's free speech, depending on the tone. — EW
- Expositor's: God cannot mean to crush him. The blow is a friend's "correction," not an enemy's attack. — Expositor's
- From Spurgeon's Treasury: "thy plague and mine." God sent it, and David deserved it. — Spurgeon

**v. 11**
- The pain of correction is how God gave David a hunger for this wisdom. — EW
- God's "rebukes" are meant to teach and warn (Job 36:8–10). Like a moth in cloth, his displeasure eats away whatever a person prizes. "Every man is vanity" works as a refrain closing each half of the psalm. — Pulpit
- Gill tells apart wrathful rebukes on the world and loving fatherly chastening of God's children. Both are for personal sin. The Greek and Latin versions read "as a spider." — Gill
- Calvin: the Hebrew word means a man of valour or excellence. Even the strongest come to nothing under God's wrath. — Calvin
- NET adopts a reading from a few manuscripts, "his beauty." — NET

**v. 12**
- David was king of Israel, yet he knew his real home was heaven. He is a stranger *with* God, not *from* God, walking with him through a hostile world (Morgan). — EW
- Tears move God to pity (Heb 5:7; 2 Kgs 20:5). We are pilgrims (Heb 11:13; 13:14), and our dependence strengthens the plea. Leviticus 25:23 is the background. — Pulpit
- Gill: a stranger to the world but known to God. It may also mean Israel living in God's land as tenants, like the patriarchs (Gen 23:4). — Gill
- NET: resident aliens depended on others' mercy, and God cared for them (Deut 24:17–22). — NET
- Illustrator: the phrase points to the passing nature of earthly things and to looking ahead to a lasting world. — Illustrator
- Guzik notes that the church appointed this psalm for funerals (citing Horne). — EW

**v. 13**
- Gill: "look away from me," echoing Job 10:20. "Be no more" means no more among the living. David still believed he would exist after death, in heaven. — Gill
- The Pulpit: he no longer wants to die and only asks for a breathing space. The verse tells us nothing either way about whether he expected a future life. — Pulpit
- NET: "turn your angry gaze away." The verb form is uncertain. — NET
- *Contrast:*
  - Calvin: this comes from fleshly unrest. David is wrong to ask for a pause just so he has time to die, though the prayer can also be read as acceptable: grant relief so I can commit my soul to God in peace. — Calvin
  - Henry rejects reading it as a passionate wish. He takes it as a godly request to live until grace makes him ready to die. — Henry

---

**Where interpreters really differ**
1. **Was the silence and outburst (vv. 1–3) sin?**
   - Gill (Baptist) and Calvin (Reformed) say it was: anger, a broken vow, complaint spoken aloud.
   - EW says the silence was wise and breaking it in prayer was the best response. Spurgeon is quoted suggesting the silence might have neglected a duty to praise.
   - Augustine says David himself condemned his silence "even from good."
2. **What does v. 4 ask for?**
   - Gill: an impatient wish to die.
   - Pulpit: Job-like weariness of life.
   - Calvin: irony.
   - Morgan (quoted by EW): a humble prayer to grasp how short life is.
   - Augustine: a longing for the goal, as in Philippians 3.
3. **Did the psalmist hope for life after death (vv. 7, 12–13)?**
   - Ellicott: no, that hope hadn't dawned yet.
   - Pulpit: the text doesn't say.
   - Gill and EW: yes, a heavenly home.
4. **Was v. 13 a godly prayer?**
   - Calvin: partly a fault.
   - Henry: a godly prayer.
